text: Multi-cloud doesn't have to mean active-active. Building two Kubernetes clusters that both take live traffic at once roughly doubles the operational surface area for a benefit Driftwood doesn't actually need yet. Instead, this phase keeps a primary cloud running the real workload, with the other standing by as backup and disaster recovery.

Theo recommends AKS as primary, for reasons grounded in what's already true about Driftwood's platform: identity, networking, and the managed databases these three services depend on are already Azure-native from the intermediate project. Running compute next to that existing data avoids paying cross-cloud latency on the busiest day of the year.

AWS keeps the role it already has — cross-region-replicated object storage and a standby database replica, idle under normal operation. Data flows one direction, Azure to AWS, unless a real failover happens. Re-testing that failover path itself is explicitly out of scope for this phase; it's inherited as-is.

This diagram settles which cloud runs what — it doesn't settle how the AKS cluster itself gets built, how Terraform enforces this architecture in code, or how cost and capacity get reported. Those are Lessons 4, 6, and 7's jobs, starting with building the actual AKS cluster next.
